test_title: SSC Selection Post 2025 (Matriculation Level) Official Paper (Held On: 25 Jul, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Which of the following is an example of fiscal policy in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Government spending on infrastructure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fiscal policy** in **India** refers to the use of **government revenue** collection (mainly **taxes**) and **expenditure** (spending) to influence the **economy**. It is formulated and implemented by the **Ministry of Finance**.
 
• **Government spending on infrastructure** is a classic example of **fiscal policy**. When the government invests in **roads**, **highways**, **railways**, and **power plants**, it directly increases **aggregate demand** and creates **employment**. ***Hence, this statement is correct.***
 
• **Adjusting repo rates** is a tool of **monetary policy**, not **fiscal policy**. This action is taken by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** to control **inflation** and **liquidity** in the banking system. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Regulating foreign exchange rates** involves interventions by the **RBI** in the **forex market** to maintain the stability of the **Indian Rupee (INR)** against **global currencies** like the **US Dollar**. This falls under **monetary and external sector management**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Controlling money supply** is the primary objective of **monetary policy**. The **RBI** uses various instruments like **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** to manage the amount of **money** circulating in the **economy**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Fiscal Policy**:
 
 
• **Expansionary Fiscal Policy**: The government **increases spending** or **decreases taxes** to stimulate **economic growth**, often used during **recessions**.
 
• **Contractionary Fiscal Policy**: The government **decreases spending** or **increases taxes** to slow down **economic growth** and combat high **inflation**.
 
 
 
• **Components of Fiscal Policy**:
 
 
• **Taxation**: Includes **Direct Taxes** (like **Income Tax** and **Corporate Tax**) and **Indirect Taxes** (like **Goods and Services Tax - GST**, introduced in **2017**).
 
• **Public Expenditure**: Spending on **subsidies**, **salaries**, **defense**, and **developmental projects** like the **National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP)** which aims for an investment of **₹111 lakh crore**.
 
• **Public Debt**: The **borrowings** made by the **government** to fund the **fiscal deficit**.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003**: This **Act** was enacted to institutionalize **financial discipline**, reduce **India's fiscal deficit**, and improve **public funds management**.
 
• **The Union Budget**: Under **Article 112** of the **Indian Constitution**, the **Union Budget** is referred to as the **Annual Financial Statement**. It is the primary document through which the **government** announces its **fiscal policy** for the **financial year** (**April 1 to March 31**).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Distinction between Fiscal and Monetary Policy**: While **fiscal policy** is handled by the **Government of India** (focusing on **spending and taxes**), **monetary policy** is the domain of the **RBI** (focusing on **interest rates and money supply**).
 
• **Major Infrastructure Schemes**: Examples include **PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan** launched in **2021**, **Bharatmala Pariyojana** for **highways**, and **Sagarmala** for **port-led development**. These represent massive **fiscal outlays** to boost the **economy**.
 
• **Deficit Financing**: When the **government expenditure** exceeds its **revenue**, it creates a **fiscal deficit**. In **India**, this is usually expressed as a **percentage** of the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**. For the **year 2023-24**, the **target** was set at **5.9%** of **GDP**.
 
• **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)**: This is a **fiscal tool** used to transfer **subsidies** directly into the **bank accounts** of **beneficiaries**, reducing **leakages** and improving the **efficiency** of **government spending**.
